summary:
The user in Farmer Mode enters the location of their field (location), whether or not it has access to irrigation and what kind of soil is there, as well as any equipment they have to utilize. using live nasa power climate information and soilgrid soil map information, terra memoria evaluates suitability for 59 different crops based on the input entered by the user. terra memoria then provides an evaluation of the suitability of each crop based on one of three criteriasuitable, with 
caution or risky. users may also evaluate two crops side-by-side in terms of yield potential, water usage and marketing potential, and run "what if" scenarios (e.g., a dry well or +2°C of warming). users can also receive recommendations for a three year crop rotation. terra memoria will provide the user with a recommendation for the amount of water needed for each crop per day according to fao-56 guidelines. since terra memoria is relying solely on fao eco-crop data, the user will be able to view the data for all recommended crops. if fao eco-crop does not provide the necessary data for a particular crop, terra memoria will indicate that fact instead of making a guess. as water shortages continue to increase globally, being able to see the trade-off between yield and water prior to planting allows farmers to make better decisions regarding when to plant, whereas ultimately it remains their decision.
details:
What it does and how it works

TERRA MEMORIA (“the memory of the soil”) is a bilingual (Turkish/English) decision-support web app built for the “Field Shift: Adapting Farms with NASA Data” challenge. It opens in Farmer Mode, a simple, touch-friendly flow:

  1. Where is your field? The farmer picks the field on a map or shares their location. The app pulls NASA POWER climate data live and explains it in plain words: rainfall against crop water need, frost days and hot days.
  2. Describe your field. The farmer enters irrigation and soil (suggested from SoilGrids), the current crop, the market and the machinery they can use.
  3. Which crops fit? The engine runs 59 crops through a monthly soil-water balance. It uses FAO-56 crop coefficients, FAO-33 yield response and Hargreaves–Samani evapotranspiration. Each crop gets a 0–100 score, a Suitable / With care / Risky label and plain-language reasons.
  4. Compare. The farmer puts up to three crops side by side on yield potential, irrigation need, water productivity, market fit and nitrogen left in the soil.
  5. Before you sow. What-if scenarios show what changes before anything is planted: warming of +1 to +3 °C, less rain, a dry well or missing machinery. A three-year rotation is also suggested.

Expert Mode gives agronomists the full technical view. It includes NASA GIBS layer comparisons (MODIS, SMAP, GPM IMERG, GRACE-FO, SRTM) and 75 m in-field layers for erosion, water stress and frost pockets. It also compares the current rotation with optimised strategies across seven criteria.

Benefits

  • Field-specific answers from free, global NASA data, with no sensors or installation. It works on a phone.
  • Yield and water trade-offs side by side. On the Konya Plain, sugar beet reaches 91% yield potential but needs 763 mm of irrigation. Winter vetch reaches 90% with 19 mm and leaves nitrogen in the soil.
  • Honest data. Every value is labelled as observed, farmer input or modelled. Newly added crop data comes only from FAO EcoCrop and FAO-56, and missing values are shown as “no data”.
  • If a NASA service is down, the app keeps working with clearly labelled backup data.

Intended impact

We want to help farmers in water-stressed regions shift to crops and rotations that fit a changing climate. The goals are to pump less groundwater, keep soil covered and protect a year’s work before sowing. For a rainfed field on the Konya Plain, the suggested rotation cuts bare soil from 7 months to 1 a year. It also fixes 55 kg/ha of nitrogen and raises climate resilience from 30% to 52%. The tool supports the farmer’s judgement and the local agronomist; it does not replace them.

Tools and technologies

  • Front end: HTML, CSS and vanilla JavaScript with no build step; Tailwind CSS, Leaflet (maps), Chart.js (charts).
    • NASA POWER API (climatology and a 2016–2025 monthly series)
    • NASA GIBS
    • ORNL DAAC MODIS NDVI (MOD13Q1)
    • GRACE-FO
    • SRTM
    • ISRIC SoilGrids
    • FAO EcoCrop
    • FAO-56 tables
  • Python: the local server, a reproducible crop-data build script and a regression test server. A browser regression suite of 168 cases keeps results identical bit for bit.
  • Hosting and hardware: hosted on Vercel, code on GitHub. No special hardware; it runs in any modern browser.

Creativity

  • One question-driven screen in plain language instead of dashboards full of indices. The full science is one click away.
  • Real data becomes imagery. Ten years of NASA POWER data become tree rings, crop root depths become root profiles and SRTM elevation becomes 3D terrain.
  • Machinery access feeds directly into the crop score, so advice matches what the farmer can actually do.

What our team considered

  • Farmers’ real constraints: water, machinery, market and soil, plus users with low digital experience (large touch targets, plain language, two languages).
  • Scientific honesty: no invented numbers, visible data gaps, and results framed as estimates.
  • Accessibility and reliability: works on phones, labels never rely on colour alone, a reduced-motion setting, and fallbacks when data services fail.
  • Ethics: the final decision always stays with the farmer.
